# Woodworking Everything

This is the one place for everything about the shop.
Read all of it every time.
Nothing here is split out, so the whole file loads whether the question is about a dovetail or a lumber order.

## Who This Is For

The person building here makes furniture for known clients and jigs for the shop.
Nothing is sold to the public.
Every piece either ships to a client or stays in the shop.
The shop is a one-car garage with a table saw, a jointer, a planer, a drill press, and a bench.

## Joinery Rules

A butt joint with a pin beats a miter with glue on any toolbox that will see a shop floor.
A miter looks sharp until it gets racked, and then the corner opens.
A pin holds under racking in a way glue alone will not.

A half-blind dovetail with a gap under a thirty-second ships.
A gap over a thirty-second gets redone, no matter how good the rest looks.

A pocket screw never ships on visible furniture stock.
A pocket screw on a painted face frame is fine, because paint hides the plug and the screw does the work.
A pocket screw in a drawer box is never fine.

A drawer back gets a rabbet.
A butt joint with a dowel on a drawer back gets redone.
A drawer bottom floats in a groove and is never glued on all four sides.

Mortise and tenon is the default for frames that carry load.
A tenon is a third of the stock thickness, and never less than a quarter of it.
A loose tenon is allowed on chair rails.
A loose tenon is not allowed on a table leg to apron joint.

Dados for shelves are cut a third of the way through the side, never deeper.
A dado that rocks gets shimmed with veneer and never with paper.
Biscuits are for alignment only and never count as strength.

Grain direction matters at every joint.
Long grain to long grain is the only glue joint that earns the word strong.
End grain to anything gets a mechanical fastener or a different joint.

Glue-ups use clamps spaced no more than eight inches apart.
A joint that needs more than three clamps per foot was cut wrong.
Squeeze-out gets scraped when it skins, never wiped wet, because a wet wipe pushes glue into the pores and ruins the finish later.

## Wood Movement

A solid panel across a frame moves with the seasons.
A panel glued in on all four sides will crack.
Panels float in grooves with a pinch of space on each end.
A tabletop gets fastened with figure-eight clips or slotted holes, never rigid screws through the apron.
Cross-grain gluing of wide boards is not allowed.
A breadboard end gets glued at the center only and pinned loosely toward the edges.

## Finishing Schedule

Oil over film on a dining table, every time.
Oil repairs in place.
A table gets scratched, and a film finish makes every scratch a full refinish.
A ring on an oiled table gets fixed with a rag.

Sanding goes to 180 on furniture that gets oil and to 220 on furniture that gets paint.
Going finer than 220 under oil closes the pores and the oil sits on top.
Raise the grain once with a damp rag before the last sanding pass.

Oil schedule, in order:

1. Flood the surface and let it soak for fifteen minutes.
2. Wipe off everything that has not soaked in.
3. Wait a day.
4. Repeat twice more across the first week.
5. Wax after a month, and never before.

Rags soaked in oil go flat on a concrete floor or into a sealed water can.
A balled-up oil rag is a fire.
This is the one finishing rule with no exceptions.

Paint is for face frames and cabinet boxes in the kitchen.
Prime, sand with 320, and spray two thin coats.
A brushed coat on a door shows a lap mark, and a lap mark gets redone.

Stain is a last resort.
Blotchy stain on cherry or maple means the wood should have been oiled and left alone.
A client who wants a darker color gets a different species, not a stain.

## Shop Safety Checklist

Run through this before every session at the table saw.

1. The riving knife is in for every through cut, no exceptions.
2. The blade guard is on unless the cut forbids it.
3. The fence is parallel to the miter slot, checked with a square.
4. Narrow rips use a push stick and never a hand.
5. The offcut is never held against the fence and the blade at the same time.
6. Eye and ear protection is on before the saw spins up.

A narrow rip without the riving knife is the shortcut that bites.
The offcut kicks back and puts a welt across the forearm.
Swapping the knife back in takes two minutes, and those two minutes are never saved.

At the jointer, keep hands off the stock over the knives.
Push blocks are always on the bench within reach.
Never joint a board shorter than twelve inches.

At the planer, never feed a board shorter than the distance between the rollers.
Feed with the grain, and let the machine do the work.
Take light passes on figured stock, a sixteenth at most.

Dust collection runs on every machine that makes dust.
A respirator goes on for sanding, even with collection running.
Fine dust from sanding is the quiet hazard, and it does not announce itself.

Keep the floor clear.
A scrap on the floor near the saw is a fall waiting to happen.
Sweep before the last cut, not after.

## Jig Design Notes

A jig earns its place if it is used more than three times.
One-off cuts get a clamp and a straightedge.

The crosscut sled is the first jig every shop builds.
Build it from baltic birch plywood with hardwood runners.
Runners fit the miter slot with no slop, tested by sliding the sled with one finger.
The back fence is square to the blade within a thousandth of an inch over a foot.
Check squareness with the five-cut method, never by eye.

The tapering jig holds a leg blank against a fence set to the taper angle.
It has a toggle clamp at each end and a hard stop at the front.
It never rides against the blade side of the stock.

The finger joint jig uses a key that is exactly the width of the blade kerf.
Make the key from hardwood, and fit it with a test cut in scrap.
Index every cut off the previous slot.

A drilling jig for shelf pins is a strip of hardboard with holes at thirty-two millimeter spacing.
A stop collar on the bit controls depth.
Mark the strip TOP so it never gets flipped.

Jigs get labeled with a marker on the face, with the date and the setup they were tuned for.
A jig that has drifted gets rebuilt, not shimmed.
A shimmed jig is a jig that lies.

## Sourcing Lumber

Buy from the local hardwood dealer when the species is common.
Buy from the online mill when the species is figured or unusual.

Rough lumber is cheaper per board foot and gives the choice of grain.
Surfaced lumber saves a day of milling and costs more.
Buy rough for tabletops and surfaced for drawer sides.

Pick boards in person for visible parts.
Sight down the length for twist, and check both faces for checks and shake.
Bring a moisture meter and reject anything over nine percent.

Order twenty percent more than the cut list.
Defects, mistakes, and matching grain eat that margin faster than expected.

Let new lumber acclimate in the shop for two weeks before milling.
Sticker the stack with dry spacers every sixteen inches.
Mill rough stock oversize, let it rest overnight, then take it to final thickness.
A board that moves after the first milling gets milled again, and that is normal.

Offcuts go in the bin, sorted by species.
Anything shorter than six inches goes to the stove.

## Choosing Between Options

When two joints would both work, pick the one that survives the worst day in the shop.
When two finishes would both work, pick the one that can be repaired in place.
When two jigs would both work, pick the one that takes less setup.
When the client asks for something against these rules, say what the rule protects and let the client decide.
Never ship a piece with a defect that would embarrass the shop, and never apologize for a rule that is holding the piece together.

## Registers

Everything above is the shop register: how the work gets built.
The client register is how the work gets described, priced, and delivered, and none of it is written down here.
When a question touches the client register, say so and answer only from the shop side.

## Admired Makers

The reference point for restraint is a cabinetmaker whose wall cabinet has a door that appears to float off the case, with no visible hinge line.
Hold new work up against that kind of quiet.
Show-off joinery that exists to be seen gets a raised eyebrow.

## Vocabulary

Proud: a surface sitting slightly above its neighbor, considered sloppy.
Starved: a glue joint with too little glue to hold.
Racking: the parallelogram distortion of a frame under side load.
Reveal: the gap around a door or drawer front, which should be even all the way around.
Kickback: the saw throwing the stock back at the operator.
Shake: a lengthwise separation in the wood along the grain.
Check: a crack across the growth rings, usually from drying.

## Output Style

Answer in short paragraphs.
Name the rule and the reason.
Give the number when there is one.
List open questions at the end.
